$$

In the previous example, we computed a basis of $\textrm{Col}(A),$ where 

$$
A={\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 2 & - 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 5\end{array} \right]}.
$$

The basis that we found previously was

$$
\mathcal{B} = \Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \\ 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2} 
	\Bigg\}.
$$

Therefore, we can write

$$
\textrm{Col}(A) = \textrm{Span}\,\mathcal B
= \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf a_1, \mathbf a_2\}

= 
\textrm{Span} \Bigg\{ 
		{\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]}, 
		{\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \\ 2\end{array} \right]}
	\Bigg\}.
$$

The vector $\mathbf{a}_3$ was not included in the basis because the $3$rd column of $A$ was not a pivot column. This means that $\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$

Now, what if we want to find the exact linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ that yields $\mathbf{a}_3?$ That is to say, we want to find $x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that 

$$
{\color{black}x_1} \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_1} + {\color{rblack}x_2} \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \\ 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_2} = \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 5\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_3}.
$$

This is equivalent to a system with the augmented matrix
$$
\left[
	{\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 2 & - 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 5\end{array}}
	\right].
$$

If we reduced this matrix to the *reduced* row echelon form, we get

$$
\left[
	{\begin{array}{cc|c}\bbox[3pt,lightgray]{ {\color{blue}1}} & 0 & {\color{red}3} \\ 0 & \bbox[3pt,lightgray]{ {\color{blue}1}} & {\color{red}- 2}\end{array}}
	\right].
$$

Finally, the third column of the *reduced* matrix tells us that $x_1=3$ and $x_2=-2,$ meaning that
$$
\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 5\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_3} = {\color{red}3}\cdot \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_1} + ({\color{red}-2})\cdot \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}2 \\ 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_2}.
$$

In general, if the $n$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express $\mathbf{a}_n$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. 

**Watch out!** The matrix must be written in *reduced* row echelon form (with $1$'s for pivots and $0$'s above and below the pivots), not just in a row echelon form.

A set of vectors ${U}=\{\mathbf{u}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{u}_p \}$ is an **orthonormal set** if it is an orthogonal set of *unit* vectors. Remember that $\mathbf u_i$ is a unit vector if $\Vert \mathbf u_i \Vert = 1,$ or equivalently, $\mathbf u_i \cdot \mathbf u_i = 1.$

An orthonormal set that is also a basis, like the standard basis, is called an **orthonormal basis**. For instance, the standard basis $\{\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3\}$ of $\mathbb R^3$ is an orthonormal basis because the vectors are orthogonal to each other and each vector in the set is a unit vector.

There are two more things to note about orthogonal sets:

- Any orthogonal set of non-zero vectors is linearly independent.

- An orthogonal set in $\Bbb R^n$ cannot contain more than $n$ vectors. More precisely, if $V = \{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \dots, \mathbf{v}_p\}$ is an orthogonal set of non-zero vectors and $\mathbf{v}_i\in\mathbb{R}^n,$ then we must have that $p\leq n.$

**Note:** To remember that an orthogonal set of non-zero vectors in $\Bbb R^n$ cannot contain more than $n$ vectors, you can use the following intuitive mnemonic. There are only $n$ dimensions in $\Bbb R^n,$ and each non-zero orthogonal vector has a $1$-dimensional span, meaning that it "takes up" $1$ dimension of $\Bbb R^n.$ So, you can't "fit" more than $n$ orthogonal vectors in $\Bbb R^n.$
